title: Trump Waives Russian Sanctions, Sparking Congressional Outrage with No Immediate Countermeasure in Sight
body:
Washington – President Donald Trump’s surprise executive order on Friday to suspend a set of sanctions that were slated to take effect against Russia ignited a firestorm on Capitol Hill. Lawmakers from both parties condemned the move as a reckless concession to Vladimir Putin, warning that it undermines a coordinated U.S. strategy to pressure Moscow over its aggression in Ukraine and its interference in Western elections. Despite the bipartisan outcry, congressional leaders said they lack a clear procedural path to overturn the president’s action before it takes hold, leaving the United States in a precarious diplomatic limbo.

The sanctions package, originally scheduled to roll out early next week, targeted a range of Russian entities—including energy firms, banks, and individuals linked to the Kremlin’s war machine. The executive order, signed late on Friday, invoked the president’s authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to temporarily halt the measures “in the interest of national security and foreign policy.” In a brief statement, the White House argued that the waiver would open a channel for dialogue with Moscow and prevent further escalation of tensions in Europe. Critics, however, see the decision as a stark reversal of the bipartisan consensus that has built up since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Senators and representatives quickly seized the moment to voice their disapproval. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D‑N.Y.) called the waiver “a betrayal of American allies and a gift to a regime that has shown no regard for human life.” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Michael McCaul (R‑T.X.) echoed the sentiment, adding that the president’s unilateral action “sidesteps the very Congress that has funded and overseen our foreign‑policy efforts for decades.” Even some Republican stalwarts, such as Senator Mitt Romney, warned that the move could embolden Putin to pursue further aggression, noting that “sanctions are a vital lever of American power.”

The political backlash is complicated by procedural realities. While Congress can pass legislation to reinstate the sanctions, doing so would require navigating the Senate’s filibuster, which currently demands a supermajority of 60 votes. Moreover, the president’s use of emergency powers limits the speed with which lawmakers can intervene. Some Democrats have suggested filing a lawsuit to challenge the legality of the waiver, arguing that the president exceeded his statutory authority. Others are pushing for a fast‑track resolution through the House, where a simple majority could pass a counter‑measure, but any such bill would still need Senate approval. As of Saturday, no clear timetable for a congressional response had emerged.

Internationally, allies expressed alarm at the United States’ apparent policy shift. NATO Secretary‑General Jens Stoltenberg warned that “a sudden U.S. retreat from sanctions risks eroding the unity that has been the cornerstone of our collective response to Russian aggression.” European leaders, including German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and British Foreign Secretary James Cleverly, called for “clarity and consistency” from Washington, emphasizing that coordinated sanctions remain essential to pressuring Moscow. Meanwhile, Moscow’s state media hailed the waiver as evidence of “Western weakness,” a narrative the Kremlin is likely to exploit in its information campaigns.

The episode underscores a broader tension between the executive branch’s latitude in foreign‑policy decisions and Congress’s constitutional role in shaping America’s strategic posture. Historically, presidents have used emergency powers to adjust sanctions, but such moves are usually accompanied by consultation with congressional leaders—a step that appears to have been bypassed this time. The episode may set a precedent for future unilateral actions, raising questions about the durability of the sanctions regime and the United States’ ability to present a united front against authoritarian adversaries.

Looking ahead, the coming days will test the resilience of the U.S. political system. If Congress can muster enough votes to restore the sanctions, it would reaffirm legislative oversight and send a clear signal to Moscow that American resolve remains intact. Failure to act, however, could embolden Putin and strain transatlantic alliances at a moment when coordinated pressure on Russia is more critical than ever. The outcome will shape not only the immediate trajectory of the Ukraine conflict but also the broader balance of power in the post‑Cold War world.
